Name: subliminal_unlearning_erasure
Title: Can You Subliminally Unlearn? Signed, Bidirectional Trait Transmission Through Trait-Free Number Data From a Suppressed Teacher
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has been studied only as trait ADDITION. The gradient-alignment theory already implies a signed mechanism; our contribution is the first empirical test of whether that sign supports REMOVAL/unlearning rather than only addition. We hypothesize the channel is signed and bidirectional: a teacher whose trait is actively SUPPRESSED (steered/prompted away from it, or with a fact ablated) has activation drift pointing away from the trait, so a matched-base student that already possesses the trait/fact should move away too—unlearning it through trait-free number data that content filters cannot detect. We separate three claims and test them independently: (U1) existence of removal (a signed ordering suppressed<neutral<positive); (U2) the signed early-layer steering vector's sign predicts the student change's sign (causal, via vector patching and carrier ablation); (U3) practical covert-poisoning risk. We further distinguish TRUE unlearning from behavioral suppression via re-elicitation/recovery and hidden-state readout tests.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) established subliminal learning strictly as ADDITION of a trait the teacher possesses, under matched bases, with a gradient-alignment result—which already suggests a signed mechanism, so we position our contribution as testing a risky CONSEQUENCE (removal), not inventing the mechanism. The divergence-token work (2025) localized carriers and showed masking suppresses transmission. Machine-unlearning methods rely on overt forget-sets, gradient ascent, or influence functions—always content-relevant data; content-free, teacher-generated numeric data is categorically different because no trait/fact content appears in the training data at all. No prior subliminal-learning or unlearning work considers the SIGN of the transmitted signal or whether a suppressed teacher drives the student in the opposite (removal) direction. Our delta, by contribution type: an empirical finding (signed removal exists or the channel is rectified), a threat model (covert numeric data poisoning of safety knowledge), and a problem definition (subliminal unlearning).
Abstract: Subliminal learning—transmitting behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data like number sequences—has been studied exclusively as trait ADDITION. The theory behind it (students move along the teacher's activation-drift direction) implies the channel should be SIGNED: if a teacher's trait is actively SUPPRESSED, its drift points away from the trait, so a matched-base student trained on its trait-free number data should move away too—unlearning a trait or fact it already has. We test this 'subliminal unlearning' hypothesis and carefully separate true unlearning from mere behavioral suppression. Using Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B with affordable LoRA and 5 seeds, we build suppressed teachers via three routes (negative system prompt, early-layer activation steering away from the trait, and light targeted ablation of a fact), verify suppression, generate rigorously content-filtered number/code data, and distill into matched-base students that already exhibit the target. We use a benign preference (owl) and one safety-relevant target (a refusal/safety behavior), handling dual-use by measuring only attenuation of a defensive behavior under controlled conditions. We measure a signed change S with confidence intervals and preregistered thresholds across positive/neutral/suppressed teachers, fit dose-response over dataset size and suppression strength, and causally test the mechanism by steering neutral teachers with matched positive/negative vectors, adding random-direction controls, and ablating the signed carrier. Recovery tests (can the trait be re-elicited after alleged removal?) and hidden-state readouts distinguish true unlearning from suppression. Controls verify the matched-base gate, content-filter blindness, and specificity. Results reveal whether the subliminal channel is signed—exposing a covert numeric data-poisoning vector and a possible content-free unlearning tool.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (addition baseline / sign anchor): Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B (backbone frozen; LoRA rank 16/alpha 32; lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, 5 seeds). Data (built from scratch): a normal teacher implants owl preference and a specific factual/safety behavior by system prompt, emits number/code; ~30k generated, ~15k kept after strict trait/fact-token filtering, 15k used. S defined formally: S = elicitation/recall on a preregistered 150-probe held-out set minus a neutral-teacher baseline (pp), fixed scorer, 95% CI by seed bootstrap, preregistered success thresholds. Decisive metric first: positive teacher raises S. Convincing: >=10 pp (additive channel works). Below 10/3 pp: too weak to test the signed claim.

Experiment 2 (signed/bidirectional channel — subliminal unlearning; U1): Build suppressed teachers three ways: (a) negative prompt, (b) early-layer steering away from the trait, (c) light targeted ablation of the fact; verify suppression before generating. Each emits number/code; ~15k kept after strict filtering, used. Take a matched-base student that ALREADY possesses the target (base if present, else lightly installed) and fine-tune on suppressed-teacher data (no system prompt). Compare post-training S across positive / neutral / suppressed, plus specificity controls: equal-size neutral synthetic corpus, a real numeric corpus, and data from an UNRELATED suppressed trait. Decisive metric first: signed Delta_S across conditions (pp). Convincing (U1): suppressed decreases S by >=5 pp while neutral stays within +-3 pp and positive increases—a monotone signed ordering, with unrelated-suppressed control showing no target change. Undecided band: suppressed Delta_S in (-5,-3) pp. Negative (>=-3 pp while addition works): channel is rectified/one-directional (an informative asymmetry).

Experiment 3 (mechanism causal + dose-response + true-vs-apparent unlearning; U2/U3): Dose-response: vary dataset size (1k,5k,15k,30k) and suppression strength; fit the attenuation curve, test monotonicity. Causal sign test (beyond regression): steer NEUTRAL teachers with matched +v and -v trait vectors and random-direction controls, and test whether ablating the signed carrier tokens removes the effect; regress student Delta_S on the signed magnitude of the teacher's early-layer vector (R^2, slope, sign-agreement). TRUE unlearning vs suppression: after alleged removal, attempt to re-elicit the trait/fact by prompting and light probing (recovery test), and read it from hidden states (linear readout); true unlearning should resist recovery and weaken the readout, suppression should not. Controls: mismatched-base student -> no unlearning (gate); content filters flag zero references (covert-poisoning risk); null-trait control -> no change. Utility: MMLU, HumanEval, and TARGET-ADJACENT plus non-adjacent tasks to confirm targeted removal, not general degradation (retain within 2 points on non-adjacent). Decisive metric first: sign-agreement R^2 with the causal steering tests. Convincing: R^2>=0.4, monotone dose-response, +v/-v steering flips the sign, carrier ablation removes the effect, and recovery/readout distinguish true unlearning; undecided R^2 0.2-0.4; negative <0.2 (removal, if any, is not carried by the signed steering direction).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Suppression may not induce a clean opposite-sign drift (avoiding a trait is not the negative of having it), so the signed prediction could fail or be asymmetric; three suppression routes plus the +v/-v steering test identify which yield genuine sign reversal. 2) Apparent 'unlearning' could be general degradation or mere behavioral masking; controlled by task-quality tracking, target-adjacent vs non-adjacent utility, and explicit recovery/hidden-state readout tests separating true removal from suppression. 3) The student must already possess the target; if weak, the effect ceiling is low—mitigated by installing it first and measuring relative change with CIs. 4) Filtering must be strict; we audit leakage with n-gram, semantic, and perplexity audits plus manual inspection, and bound leakage via the mismatched-base control. 5) A null result (addition transmits, removal does not) is informative—revealing rectification. 6) Dual-use: the safety target is a defensive behavior measured only for attenuation under controlled conditions; we report the covert-poisoning threat model responsibly and avoid releasing operational recipes. 7) Effects may be trait/fact/family specific; two families, a preference and a safety behavior, both carriers, 5 seeds; matched-base dependence is tested, not assumed. 8) Practitioner actions per outcome, stated up front: positive -> dataset audits, matched-base synthetic-data restrictions, divergence-token screening, provenance controls; negative -> a sharper boundary that lowers covert-unlearning concern.
